reviews.text: Charlotte Wells's feature debut, a heartbreaking portrait of a father and daughter, is an ode to memory that dotingly recalls the texture and details of a childhood holiday.
reviews.author: Christina Newland

reviews.text: Wells seeks to capture the nostalgia and dilemmas of everyday life over a fixed discourse on the loss of innocence and paternal sacrifices, but his narrative remains situated in common places where the emotional hook is absent. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: Poignant and anchored by Mescal and Corio’s terrific performances, Aftersun is an outstanding debut from Charlotte Wells that quickly confirms her directing talents.
reviews.author: Daniel Allen

reviews.text: Its striking imagery evokes both the power of memory and its obscurities through the ingenious use of analog video and purposeful audio/visual distortions.
reviews.author: Marya E. Gates

reviews.text: Aftersun is a sad and beautiful exploration of grief, of Sophie's struggle to reconcile complex and conflicting feelings about her father, and her struggle to forgive his decision, and perhaps to forgive herself.
reviews.author: Valentina Morillo

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ stunning debut is a quiet rumination of the lost daughter.
reviews.author: Srivatsan S

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ picture-perfect debut visually epitomizes the heart-wrenching processes of memory.
reviews.author: Prabhjot Bains

reviews.text: Director Charlotte Wells gives us one of the most piercing debuts in recent memory with this intimate dad-daughter relationship drama.
reviews.author: Gautam Sunder

reviews.text: Shimmering like a mirage that retreats and dematerializes the closer one gets, Aftersun may just be the best movie of 2022.
reviews.author: Greg Carlson

reviews.text: Aftersun is so interesting in the way it explores the reality of parents that they keep their children in the dark about.
reviews.author: Jillian Chilingerian

reviews.text: Aftersun is left open-ended, and that’s a perfect conclusion to this portrait of a father and daughter relationship. It speaks to the inability of a child to truly understand their parents, no matter how valiantly they try.
reviews.author: Tina Kakadelis

reviews.text: 'Aftersun' depicts an unvarnished portrait of a young man grappling with responsibilities, struggling to hold on to his own life while willingly shouldering responsibility of another.
reviews.author: Ishita Sengupta

reviews.text: Aftersun is a tour de force for its two leads, a phenomenal child performance from Frankie Corio with Paul Mescal cementing himself as one of the best actors of his generation and showcasing incredible range
reviews.author: Christopher Connor

reviews.text: In addition, there’s a dark side to all of this; you begin to remember the darkest of memories – the ones you try to avoid...
reviews.author: Hector A. Gonzalez

reviews.text: The Scottish director is not only beautifully attuned to the most minor nuances of human sensitivities, but also capable of translating this natural inclination through a refined command over form.
reviews.author: Rafaela Sales Ross

reviews.text: Without being an overtly dramatic or narrative lesson, Aftersun sticks a finger into the wound and digs into the most intimate to devastating effect. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Mauricio Jarufe Caballero

reviews.text: The film is small, discreet, intimate, a little coy—at times, a bit self-involved and inward-turning. The somewhat self-conscious insistence on the lack of great drama can be tedious at times.
reviews.author: David Walsh

reviews.text: The easy pace of Wells’s direction brings out the best in her central performers, and the chemistry between Mescal and Corio plays out effortlessly. The light moments between them are warm and the darker ones linger heavily.
reviews.author: Anna Bogutskaya

reviews.text: A quiet, emotionally unmooring portrait of father and daughter in moments of blissful silliness and small confessions... it’s a devastatingly honest rendition of the aftershocks of a parent’s love when we realise, too late, the simple joys we shared.
reviews.author: Stephen A. Russell

reviews.text: Wells shows how interactions that were solid within their own moment become more ambiguous as time has gone by and the adult understanding of Sophie has grown.
reviews.author: Amber Wilkinson

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’s self-assured debut takes pains to be specific to its time and place.
reviews.author: A.S. Hamrah

reviews.text: A subtlety—a nuanced exposition of storylines that might have easily been too simplified—that one doesn’t often find in larger films, particularly American ones...
reviews.author: Daphne Merkin

reviews.text: The role calls for the sensitivity of the budding artist, the impishness of childhood, the yearning of adolescence, security and sudden insecurity, the unspoken intimacy of parent and child. Corio is marvelous.
reviews.author: Daniel Drake

reviews.text: For a movie that initially seemed slight upon first glance, this has haunted me like few other films from 2022.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: Aftersun can be momentarily cathartic in making us confront the troubling ghosts of our past that tend to define our present. But it doesn't offer the false promise of healing in the future.
reviews.author: Namrata Joshi

reviews.text: By embracing the polysemous instead of rushing to define her lead character, Wells has given us a feature that exists somewhere between capital-Q queer cinema and a more lowercase approach.
reviews.author: Billy McEntee

reviews.text: Aftersun is a stealthy movie because even as it lulls you into a state where you’re wondering just what is the point of the whole endeavour, it has already successfully gripped you with its unsentimental heart.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: It’s a very personal piece and much about it is more mystifying than revelatory. Still, the leads are magnificent together. If nothing else, Aftersun will make you think about your relationship with your own father.
reviews.author: Eleanor Ringel Cater

reviews.text: Dreamy, deft and light on detail, this elusive tale of memory and loss has a playful summer-holiday home movie look and a compelling emotional resonance
reviews.author: Jane Freebury

reviews.text: Sadness is an all-pervasive threat in a paradoxically lovely debut from writer-director Charlotte Wells, based in part on her life.
reviews.author: Andiee Paviour

reviews.text: While Wells demonstrates a delicate and apparently very personal talent – she has said in interviews that her film is emotionally autobiographical – she will in the future, I hope, move on to more substantial material than this wafer-thin story.
reviews.author: David Stratton

reviews.text: Mescal gets a tilt at Hollywood's night of nights for his efforts, but Corio is just as extraordinary — perhaps more so given that it's her first acting role. Watching the duo together is a marvel.
reviews.author: Sarah Ward

reviews.text: A perfect film.
reviews.author: Simon Miraudo

reviews.text: Somehow, without its effects becoming obvious, Wells brings us to the gravity of what she is remembering. The accumulation of small details builds a strong sense of who these characters are.
reviews.author: Paul Byrnes

reviews.text: Aftersun is a bright, funny, immensely likeable and touching film.
reviews.author: Graeme Tuckett

reviews.text: Writer-director Charlotte Wells brings a lightness of touch to just about every element of this film. The relationship between father and daughter feels utterly real, sometimes at cross purposes, sometimes bored, sometimes as close as two people can be
reviews.author: Anthony Morris

reviews.text: [There] are gaps in Aftersun that are left to the audience. [… Charlotte] Wells has a keen eye for detail and feelings, one she uses to build moment upon moment into a towering emotional crescendo.
reviews.author: Akhil Arora

reviews.text: The Situationists and the Sex Pistols may have had nothing good to say about cheap holidays in other people’s misery, but Wells finds a wealth of beauty and heartache in this one.
reviews.author: Jason Anderson

reviews.text: Events play out at an unhurried pace, but the film certainly leaves a lasting emotional impression.
reviews.author: Max Copeman

reviews.text: Delicate and not rushed, the full brunt of this film’s impact didn’t strike me. However, the final scene does wrap a deft bow around the lingering mystery.
reviews.author: Dan Buffa

reviews.text: A tremendous film. Something that looks at a hard topic like depression in a very beautiful and human way.
reviews.author: Victoria Luxford

reviews.text: It’s not just a wrenching family drama but a fascinating meditation on memory, the poignant dance between past and present, and the experience of looking back on childhood with the perspective of an adult, seeing things we didn’t notice before.
reviews.author: Rob Thomas

reviews.text: What works tremendously in favour of Aftersun is the extent to which screenwriter-director Charlotte Wells is able to trust her audience to fill in the details.
reviews.author: Santanu Das

reviews.text: It combines the worst elements of a slow-moving art film and a found footage film. While there is clever camera work in the film, especially in the last scene, I found the visual elements of the film to be too repetitive and not illuminating enough.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: The delicate portrayal of how social and financial pressures impact the children of those at the sharp end of them, is what ultimately makes Aftersun so haunting and difficult to forget.
reviews.author: Nathalie Olah

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells has produced something that will have us talking for years and years to come.
reviews.author: Alberto Cox Délano

reviews.text: A hypnotic and mesmerizing quiet slice of life.
reviews.author: Lori C.

reviews.text: Wells is masterfully using the cinema form for a powerful, intimate discourse on memory and connection, as profound as Hirokazu Koreeda's 'After Life,' but subtler. It's a beautiful achievement, worthy of many viewings.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: Aftersun is a ripe, sensitive and slightly mysterious drama film served by great actors and crystallized by a rigorous staging and a deeper sense of observation.
reviews.author: Filipe Freitas

reviews.text: This father-daughter drama is a lyrical, impressionistic childhood reminiscence that weaves past and present to create the textured experience of memory.
reviews.author: Loren King

reviews.text: Aftersun is a sharply drawn memoir that captures moments of happiness shared by a father and daughter, a time that will be replayed in the mind for years to come.
reviews.author: John Lui

reviews.text: Aftersun is an acquired taste for those who like to watch raw dramatic emotions.
reviews.author: Abhishek Srivastava

reviews.text: Aftersun takes a fond look at parenthood, but doesn't hide the inherently hard moments of life. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Luis Angel H. Mora

reviews.text: Well acted and respectable for its heart, but the structure of the story and narrative feels too laissez-faire for my tastes.
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: Aftersun is a film about belonging, aching loss, and making memories, and you will find yourself taking deep dives into personal pools of these elements, looking for your share of the sun.
reviews.author: Shubhra Gupta

reviews.text: Steven Spielberg mustered the courage to confront his childhood trauma only five decades into his career (and after the perpetrators of it had both passed). Charlotte Wells has achieved something just as majestic with her first movie.
reviews.author: Rohan Naahar

reviews.text: Aftersun's warmth is so all-encompassing, it takes a while for the underlying sadness to make its presence felt. In this wistful, ultimately wrenching film, time slows down and speeds up. The biggest tragedy, however, is that it doesn't stand still.
reviews.author: Gayle Sequeira

reviews.text: The fact that this is Charlotte Wells’ feature film writing and directorial debut is stunning. Her vision is laid out meticulously, is so well-paced, and it has one of the absolute best final scenes/images of the year.
reviews.author: Aaron White

reviews.text: The pathos in Aftersun is staggering. From the opening frame, there's a lingering emotional ambiance that suggest something meaningful is about to take place. And it very much does.
reviews.author: JD Duran

reviews.text: A poetic, contemplative, elegant film with a heartbreaking story of the strong bond between a father and his daughter, this one packs quite the emotional punch.
reviews.author: Louisa Moore

reviews.text: Anchored by two outstanding lead performances, “Aftersun” snatches the past, turning a faded Polaroid into a tangible web of contentment and the inexorable ache of loss.
reviews.author: Rubén Rosario

reviews.text: An ordinary film would lead toward an explosive ending, but despite the mounting tension there is nothing plot-driven about this subtle, piercing, small wonder of a film...
reviews.author: Caryn James

reviews.text: Things are sunny on the surface, but a melancholy truth lies beneath, obscured through Sophie’s young eyes. When it finally bubbles to the surface, it packs a heartbreaking punch.
reviews.author: Ella Feldman

reviews.text: More evocatively, the film reflects on the things we never truly know about our own lives, and about the people we have loved and thought we knew so well.
reviews.author: Chuck Wilson

reviews.text: Undeniably an inspiring watch, but it's almost inevitable to walk out with emotional wounds and an empty feeling in your soul. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Randy Meeks

reviews.text: Aftersun maintains the airs of an ephemeral memory – a fleeting moment in time that simultaneously feels incredibly vivid yet hauntingly undefined.
reviews.author: Matt Conway

reviews.text: At worst, Aftersun will be the stunning piece we look back on in twenty years, knowing it was the announcement of special stars.
reviews.author: Alan French

reviews.text: Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio are mesmerizing in this unforgettable story about the infinite power of memories. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: An adult's emotional introspection; she recalls strong childhood memories to give them a more profound and serene interpretation. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Bonfil

reviews.text: Aftersun is a beautiful study of how the nature of our memories changes as our time on Earth expands our ability to see the reality of one another. [Full review in Portuguese]
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: Leaving much to speculation, Aftersun doesn’t promise any more than it can really offer, keeping its proceedings at a watchful distance even at the points where it seems most obliged to share and give.
reviews.author: George Elkind

reviews.text: Beneath the luminous surface of a summer film, one of the most devastating movies of the season emerges. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Eulàlia Iglesias

reviews.text: It doesn't have much plot but the 2 lead performances are very likable and sweet and you find yourself rooting for this pair.
reviews.author: Rachel Wagner

reviews.text: A film about paternal estrangement that goes much further than that. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: David Pardillos

reviews.text: Nostalgia through memories. "Aftersun" is one of the few movies that have been able to convey those sensations, those images that make up our childhood memories. In fact, it's that quality that gives the film its dreamlike tone. Full review in Spanish.
reviews.author: Sebastian Zavala Kahn

reviews.text: Each viewer who sees “Aftersun” will have a moment where it all clicks into place. And that moment won’t be the same moment for the person sitting next to you.
reviews.author: Sean P. Means

reviews.text: It’s strangely moving, and a joyous examination of a father/daughter relationship, but it’s ultimately too ambiguous and ephemeral to be game-changing.
reviews.author: Mike Massie

reviews.text: It’s a complex and affecting drama about the vagaries of memory and the uncertainties of family dynamics.
reviews.author: Russ Simmons

reviews.text: Wells leaves the details unspoken via a formally fluid, sensorial experience. All we really know for certain is that their love for each other was undeniable—Mescal (unforgettably vulnerable) and Corio's performances ensure it.
reviews.author: Jared Mobarak

reviews.text: Wells’ use of visual texture doesn’t just help capture her story. It resonates through that story in all directions, echoing through the medium itself, as if to turn the camera back on the nature of images, and the way we perceive them.
reviews.author: Siddhant Adlakha

reviews.text: A notable study about broken dreams and sundered futures. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Juan Pablo Russo

reviews.text: Beautiful and small and enormous.
reviews.author: Matt Pais

reviews.text: First time writer-director Charlotte Wells very nearly did an excellent job with “Aftersun,” but she didn’t trust herself to get her point across, and overdoes it so badly the whole movie spoils.
reviews.author: Sarah Manvel

reviews.text: Told with such delicacy, such empathy, that it’s impossible to leave it unchanged, "Aftersun" is bruising in effect, haunting in what it leaves us shouldering.
reviews.author: Allyson Johnson

reviews.text: Aftersun will be a movie memory to ruminate on and revisit for years to come, a perfect, personal film.
reviews.author: Eric Marchen

reviews.text: What Charlotte Wells achieves is curious, strange, and welcome...
reviews.author: Pablo O. Scholz

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ debut is a memorable one... The soft touch of idealism meets the hard grasp of reality in a tight and unrelenting grip. Mescal is quite terrific.
reviews.author: Mark Johnson

reviews.text: Wells captures with her images, truthful and painful, certain and elusive, an ambiguous atmosphere of enjoyment and melancholy. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Paula Vázquez Prieto

reviews.text: Brief, emotionally-rich moments are sandwiched between such nothingness that it’s difficult to care beyond a basic humanist level.
reviews.author: Edwin Arnaudin

reviews.text: First-time director Charlotte Wells memorializes the singular, unreal and entirely fleeting feeling of a vacation bond shared with one’s irregular guardian.
reviews.author: Chance Solem-Pfeifer

reviews.text: An emotional, striking feature debut ... Aftersun surprises with an understated, emotionally complex and nuanced portrait of the hidden, unexpressed needs of a parent ... Aftersun has unearthed an acting delight in Corio
reviews.author: Latoya Austin

reviews.text: Wells knows exactly what she’s doing, and her storytelling is as precise as it is piercing.
reviews.author: Mark Kermode

reviews.text: Wells’ direction is remarkable in its confidence and clarity. Aftersun is a visual marvel; it recreates those slightly crappy childhood holidays with precision and care, affection even.
reviews.author: Maria Lattila

reviews.text: Wells' ability to capture the innocence of her past self, from a more mature and grown-up point of view is what makes her film into such an unusual piece of filmmaking.
reviews.author: Linda Marric

reviews.text: Writer-director Charlotte Wells's feature debut Aftersun is a sublime example of how an opaque style can be wedded to an ambiguous storytelling technique without cost to psychological truth.
reviews.author: Graham Fuller

reviews.text: Aftersun is a little gem -- restrained, subtle, sweetly melancholic, and the interplay between Mescal and Corio has the unerring ring of truth.
reviews.author: Paul Whitington

reviews.text: There is so much going on in Aftersun that I might have to watch it again, and you know what? It will surely break my heart a second time.
reviews.author: Chris Wasser

reviews.text: For all that Aftersun can be described as gentle, contemplative and even beautiful, it’s also the kind of film that feels as if it’s teetering on the edge of a cliff.
reviews.author: Clarisse Loughrey

reviews.text: Aftersun excels at capturing the little moments that come to mean so much when we look back on our lives. It also makes us appreciate them even more.
reviews.author: Harry Guerin

reviews.text: The power of the film is that it lives so firmly within the ambiguity of parental feelings.
reviews.author: Kevin Maher

reviews.text: This is an experience you won’t forget in a hurry.
reviews.author: Matt Maytum

reviews.text: For some, Aftersun may simply not land. But those of us who love it will find ourselves in Sophie's situation, unable to dispel its final images from our memory.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: I had my top-five-movies-of-the-year list all sorted. Now - boom! - I’ve had to start from scratch. Damn you, Mescal, for being the cornerstone of something so beautiful.
reviews.author: Charlotte O'Sullivan

reviews.text: One of the most beautiful and affecting films I have seen this year.
reviews.author: Grant Rollings

reviews.text: …an auspicious debut, largely through Wells’ ability to get sensitive, natural performances from her leads, and through the fresh photography of Gregory Oke…
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: Aftersun captures the poignant beauty of ephemeral joy—moments our memory can miraculously suspend in time.
reviews.author: Brett McCracken

reviews.text: Paul Mescal's film is a micro-masterclass in poignancy and heartbreak...
reviews.author: Larushka Ivan-Zadeh

reviews.text: The film is the first from Scottish director Charlotte Wells, the result such a gossamer knockout that the fact seems implausible, the movie made with a dizzyingly sharp eye for the universal stuff of growing up.
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: ... tender, honest, and subtly devastating. It’s a heartfelt, affecting portrait of a father-daughter relationship that lingers in the mind afterward.
reviews.author: Valerie Kalfrin

reviews.text: So memorable and moving the first time, Aftersun is all the more affecting seen again. And again. It deserves all the prizes.
reviews.author: David Sexton

reviews.text: Wells avoids the commonplace, complacency, and demagogy to achieve something truly particular, with a degree of intimacy, tenderness, and subtlety that make this first feature film a surprise and revelation of the year. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Diego Batlle

reviews.text: This mesmeric debut will make you want to stay suspended in its sun-baked setting with its two captivating lead characters for far longer than the runtime. A triumph of new British filmmaking.
reviews.author: Beth Webb

reviews.text: The film feels like an embrace of the past, acknowledging that it’s still always present due to how we’ve retained certain memories of those we were closest to. Charlotte Wells has crafted a stunning debut about fathers & daughters I won't soon forget.
reviews.author: Jim Laczkowski

reviews.text: Memories carry with them beauty and pain in equal measure. Charlotte Wells’ assured debut is a work of bittersweet art that will now be another we carry with us for when we need it.
reviews.author: Erik Childress

reviews.text: A penetrating portrait of a daughter’s search for a father that, as a child, she barely knew...a memory piece that points to mysteries that viewers must ultimately figure out for themselves.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: This is a gentle moment, a story of growing up through the eyes of a child, and a film that captures the whimsical, yet romantic glow of the love we can have for our parents.
reviews.author: Leo Brady

reviews.text: Aftersun is a stunning debut and one of the best films of the year. One that will leave its mark and stay with you for a long time. Similar to that unwanted but inevitable holiday sunburn!
reviews.author: Dallas King

reviews.text: Though it succeeds in a number of ways, Aftersun truly triumphs thanks to the two actors at its center.
reviews.author: Lisa Trifone

reviews.text: The acting is very naturalistic, but the story is coming-of-age familiar … and moves with the pace of a snail stuck in glue. For me, there wasn't enough "there" there, but for folks with unresolved issues with absent fathers it might resonate louder.
reviews.author: Patrick McDonald

reviews.text: We see a Polaroid of father and daughter begin to develop but never come fully into focus, a powerful visual metaphor for Wells’s exploration of identity and a relationship that is just in the process of forming...
reviews.author: Adam Kempenaar

reviews.text: Thanks to Wells’s evident confidence, this story, constructed slowly and focused on small moments, is more mesmerizing than most...
reviews.author: Becca James

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells' promising debut feature plays with memory as a tool and lets its story unfold in dream-like waves.
reviews.author: Adam Graham

reviews.text: Every moment, every snippet of dialogue, every detail down to the smallest role or the tiniest detail in the background feels like a vibrant slice of real life.
reviews.author: Richard Roeper

reviews.text: Much like Normal People, Aftersun lives and dies by the chemistry between the two leads, and [Paul] Mescal and [Frankie] Corio are never less than fully convincing as father and daughter.
reviews.author: Kathy Fennessy

reviews.text: A summer vacation with no defined time frame, and where the absence of answers and words give rise to a double emotional catharsis. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Felipe Rodríguez Torres

reviews.text: Aftersun is practically the definition of a "small" movie, but it sneaks up on you.
reviews.author: A.A. Dowd

reviews.text: I don’t want to oversell it — plenty have already — because it’s a clear-eyed poem of remembering, made from material usually treated as heart-tugging prose.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: Drenched with beautiful moments as Scottish writer-director Charlotte Wells gives us a glimpse of the close bond between a father and daughter. Paul Mescal & Frankie Corio are terrific.
reviews.author: Joe Friar

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ moody story of a father and a daughter on vacation is raw and authentic. Her use of a naturalistic camera sets a sincere tone that’s uniquely engaging.
reviews.author: Jonathan W. Hickman

reviews.text: Cheers to Scotland’s Charlotte Wells for making the best movie of the year by a first-time writer-director. And cheers to Paul Mescal and young  Frankie Corio for bringing this unforgettable father-daughter story to such funny, touching and vital life.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Beyond the fine performances, there is the expressive look of it. Wells and her cinematographer, Gregory Oke ("Raf"), turn concrete images into abstract beauty that slowly resolves into rapturous visual splendor.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: Emotional, beautiful, and heartbreaking, Aftersun is perfection. In the moments of love and laughter, Wells is able to capture the sadness creeping in...
reviews.author: Kate Sánchez

reviews.text: It’s all elisions, ellipses and lingering looks that build to an almost overwhelming emotional force.
reviews.author: Sean Burns

reviews.text: Don't miss this trip.  Through careful nuance and routine occurrences, Wells threads colossal and timeless messages.
reviews.author: Jeff Mitchell

reviews.text: An exercise is subtly playing with our emotions and expectations
reviews.author: Peter Gray

reviews.text: 'Aftersun' is about memory and flows like it. It may not be the movie you expect, but it’s worthwhile.
reviews.author: Preston Barta

reviews.text: Frankie Corio gives a great performance as Sophie, one of those amazingly natural turns that makes it seem as if no acting is happening.
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: We’re on childhood time, and the clock ticks according to Sophie’s biorhythms, somehow slowed down by unspoken worry about her dad.
reviews.author: Robert Horton

reviews.text: Scottish feature debut filmmaker Charlotte Wells crafts a tenderly experimental and “emotionally autobiographical" diary of her father who died when she was just 16.
reviews.author: Jason Fraley

reviews.text: At times feeling like a junior high riff on Morvern Callar, it’s a subtle and beautiful film that uses “Under Pressure” in a way that simply owns it forever
reviews.author: Jason Shawhan

reviews.text: Aftersun is lyrical without ever being obtuse, and it's a film that flourishes when attention is paid to details.
reviews.author: Richard Whittaker

reviews.text: From its gut-wrenching script and stirring cinematography to brilliant performances from the always-spectacular Paul Mescal and newcomer Frankie Corio, Aftersun is a special one.
reviews.author: Lauren Bradshaw

reviews.text: A stunner, a heartbreaker on love, grief and the random moments in life that solidify into haunting memories.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: A tribute to father-daughter relationships and the feeling of looking back on your childhood and realizing what your parents were going through, how much they loved you, and how you'll never really know who they were.
reviews.author: Alexis Potter

reviews.text: 100 minutes of vaguely hinting at issues the film is far too discreet to reveal made for a slice-of-life drama more affected than affecting, in my book.
reviews.author: Dennis Harvey

reviews.text: There is a time, probably somewhere around 11, when your kid no longer wants to hold your hand...
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: “Aftersun” stirs powerfully inarticulate emotions of what has been given and what is owed – what we had that we missed knowing we had and what we hold on to because it’s the only thing that’s left.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Mysteries lurk at the edges of the obliquely observed, tenderly banal events.
reviews.author: Peter Keough

reviews.text: Starring Frankie Corio and Paul Mescal, Charlotte Wells’ feature debut is an emotional high-wire act, masterfully conducted with artistic vision and grounded in human nuance.
reviews.author: Noah Gittell

reviews.text: It’s a beautiful finale, so sad and so appropriate. You’ve never heard anything like it. But then, you’ve never seen anything quite like Aftersun either. So it fits.
reviews.author: Chris Knight

reviews.text: A heartbreakingly beautiful look at an 11-year-old girl’s fond, complex memories of her father.
reviews.author: Travis Hopson

reviews.text: A memory movie, not just a movie about someone’s memory but a movie about memory itself, presented in a flickering, sometimes kaleidoscopic fashion, present mingled with past, layered with understanding and regret.
reviews.author: Nell Minow

reviews.text: It’s hard to explain exactly how writer-director Charlotte Wells’s feature debut, “Aftersun,” pulls off the wave of emotion it instills in the viewer.
reviews.author: Odie Henderson

reviews.text: [T]he film's collective emotional impact is staggering.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: Mildly charming.
reviews.author: Dwight Brown

reviews.text: Aftersun is a beautiful debut film about fathers and daughters seen through the lens of memory.
reviews.author: Karen Gordon

reviews.text: Plays like a surgically precise dismantling of one’s heart. Aftersun is a richly textured father-daughter drama with hidden depth that will instantly have one combing through the memories again
reviews.author: Robert Kojder

reviews.text: A film to be experienced — just go with it — the full impact of “Aftersun” comes as the credits start to roll, and the processing begins.
reviews.author: G. Allen Johnson

reviews.text: …melancholy and mysterious.  Wells has also unearthed a huge discovery in newcomer Frankie Corio, who gives an amazingly assured and sensitive performance as the 11 year-old Sophie.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: Aftersun cuts you in two with such emotional intensity, such impressive dramatic force, that I could only sit and fight back the inevitable tears.
reviews.author: Barry Hertz

reviews.text: It’s a movie that hinges on your ability to put a big portion of yourself into it. For me that requires a deeper connection – one that comes from an understanding of the characters that (for one reason or another) I never had.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: Aftersun is perhaps the most formally intricate and complex film I’ve seen in 2022, and it rewards contemplation beyond its emotionally eviscerating effect.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Aftersun has more to offer than the usual. What it lacks in answers, it more than returns in grace.
reviews.author: K. Austin Collins

reviews.text: You feel deeply for these characters, even after only a few scenes, and Wells aptly sucks you into their world.
reviews.author: Emily Zemler

reviews.text: The subject's thoughts count more than the plot.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: The astonishingly assured directorial debut of Charlotte Wells, a Scottish filmmaker who sourced much of the script from her own autobiographical details.
reviews.author: Tanner Gordon

reviews.text: It's best if viewers know up front that Aftersun is mostly a series of 'slice of life' flashback scenes shown through videos taken during a family vacation in Turkey in the 1990s. What's more intriguing is the melancholic mystery behind these flashbacks.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: Wells masterfully weaves the past and present together, and it’s in the exploration of one’s memory where the drama is at its best.
reviews.author: Mae Abdulbaki

reviews.text: Paul Mescal is a quiet revelation in Charlotte Wells' exquisite feature directorial debut.
reviews.author: Matthew St. Clair

reviews.text: The performances here are quiet marvels.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: A work of masterful and almost unbearable melancholy.
reviews.author: Alison Willmore

reviews.text: With two masterfully understated performances and a rich visual texture, this incisive two-hander explores subtle father-daughter dynamics and the fragility of generational bonds with tenderness and offbeat charm.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: Though any honest summation can't do it justice, Charlotte Wells's tender feature debut is the kind of revelation that movie fans dream of finding: not a wow so much as a guaranteed piece of emotional ravishment.
reviews.author: Joshua Rothkopf

reviews.text: Wells, in her first feature, embraces the inherent messiness of it all perfectly. This is a collage of emotion pieced together from photographs, a souvenir rug, shaky home videos... the mind, of course, and the horrible/wonderful songs of that summer.
reviews.author: Lindsey Bahr

reviews.text: I wept buckets, because writer-director Charlotte Wells so honestly realizes Sophie and Calum, and the potency and poetry of their father-daughter connection.
reviews.author: Thelma Adams

reviews.text: In a mood-forward film, the prevailing sense is one of girlhood taking its last untroubled breath. Among other things this means agreeing, for a little longer, to overlook all the things about your dad he would prefer that you not see.
reviews.author: Michelle Orange

reviews.text: An act of imaginative empathy.
reviews.author: Sheila O'Malley

reviews.text: Frankie Corio may be the breakthrough star of the year.
reviews.author: Fletcher Peters

reviews.text: A beautifully sculpted and quietly shattering first feature from the Scottish writer-director Charlotte Wells.
reviews.author: Justin Chang

reviews.text: A remarkable, moving debut feature from Charlotte Wells.
reviews.author: Will DiGravio

reviews.text: t’s deeply felt, a warm embodiment of a liminal time in life when our conceptions of ourselves and our loved ones come pinging into focus while also, somehow, drifting into new confusion.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: The power of the film comes from its embrace of the basic and universal fact of loss.
reviews.author: A.O. Scott

reviews.text: Naturally deconstructing childhood nostalgia with a resounding rawness, Aftersun is a profound slice-of-drama that marks a compelling debut by writer/director Charlotte Wells.
reviews.author: Rendy Jones

reviews.text: Evoking the early works of Lynne Ramsay and Andrea Arnold, writer-director Charlotte Wells leaves much of the subtext up to your imagination and just allows the actors’ performances to tell the real story.
reviews.author: Jennifer Heaton

reviews.text: The ambition in [Wells's] script would be hard for any actor to pull off, but the beating heart of Aftersun comes in the form of its two leads, whose chemistry together could fool anyone into thinking they had known each other their entire life.
reviews.author: Jacob Throneberry

reviews.text: Aftersun feels like a combination of memory and hallucination, but rooted in truth.
reviews.author: Murtada Elfadl

reviews.text: This is a tough story that’s presented with beauty and grace, and it respects that not all searches have answers.
reviews.author: Emily Wheeler

reviews.text: A spellbinding, genuinely heartfelt and refreshingly un-Hollywood slice-of-life.
reviews.author: Avi Offer

reviews.text: Rumors of something remarkable have circled around “Aftersun” since its première, at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, and guess what? The rumors are true.
reviews.author: Anthony Lane

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells has delivered something emotionally unique with her debut feature Aftersun. Grounded by staggeringly understated performances from Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio, there is never a false note in this devastating family drama.
reviews.author: Martin Carr

reviews.text: For a movie so obsessed with the details of daily life, then, it was that much more disappointing when it pulled a punch at its end to merely suggest tragedy, instead of actually showing it.
reviews.author: Rich Juzwiak

reviews.text: Our brains tend to obscure, distort and falsify as well as heighten, protect and heal, depending on how you want to remember that moments or person in your life. Aftersun, is a poignant and deeply personal examination of those memories.
reviews.author: Dustin Chang

reviews.text: Wells demonstrates an impressive ability to show restraint which isn’t common in debut films, and shows her deep understanding not just of the craft but of what she wants to say.
reviews.author: Alysha Prasad

reviews.text: The effective blending of the past and the future paired with Mescal and Corio's beautifully natural performances make Aftersun a movie that will stick with you long after it's done.
reviews.author: Belen Edwards

reviews.text: Aftersun, the splash-of-cold-water debut from Charlotte Wells, is where the falsehoods of movies and memories meet. The results are nothing short of masterful.
reviews.author: Matthew Dougherty

reviews.text: 'Aftersun' pushes you to want to solve its questions while imploring you to savor the moment. It’s a delicate dance life does on its own
reviews.author: Murjani Rawls

reviews.text: Aftersun is a soul-shaking cinematic achievement with one of the best depictions of depression ever to hit the silver screen.
reviews.author: Jeff Nelson

reviews.text: Aftersun is a melancholic and compassionate look at the love between a father and daughter. A directorial debut that triumphs as one of the year’s most important cinematic experiences.
reviews.author: David Gonzalez

reviews.text: Anchored by stellar performances from Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio, filmmaker Charlotte Wells’ debut is empathetic and strikingly realized. It’s also got a late-film needle-drop for the ages.
reviews.author: Cory Woodroof

reviews.text: Both Paul Mescal and newcomer Frankie Corio are more than up to the task to bring Wells’s poetic meditations to fruition, and it's their collective efforts that ensures the ending devastates us with the weight of its impact.
reviews.author: Tomas Trussow

reviews.text: Although it feels more like a short film coaxed to feature-length, what an incredible way to start a career.
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: I didn’t want Aftersun to end—and the desire to preserve and extend moments into infinity is what the movie is all about.
reviews.author: Adam Nayman

reviews.text: A thoughtful, compassionate, and visually arresting meditation on love, memory, and the passage of time.
reviews.author: Victor Stiff

reviews.text: A father and daughter resort holiday, viewed through a prism of wistfulness and regret, takes on magical meaning in this arresting feature directing debut by Scotland’s Charlotte Wells.
reviews.author: Peter Howell

reviews.text: After all is said and done, it is films like Aftersun that will stand the test of time long after we are gone.
reviews.author: Chase Hutchinson

reviews.text: Aftersun’s slow and steady buildup culminates in its final 15 minutes, giving way to a surprisingly sharp and affecting end.
reviews.author: Hannah Lodge

reviews.text: Aftersun is a revelation, and Wells deserves all the accolades that will hopefully continue to come her way.
reviews.author: Wilson Kwong

reviews.text: Wells' extraordinary film shows just enough without telling us anything directly, an incredibly potent way to register grief and loss, and to display how much we will still never know about the people we love dearest.
reviews.author: Piers Marchant

reviews.text: ...a small-scale premise that’s employed to predominantly (and distressingly) tedious and underwhelming effect...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: … a beautiful film that heralds the emergence of a major cinematic talent.
reviews.author: Nadine Whitney

reviews.text: Aftersun is a film you follow by feeling.
reviews.author: Sarah Bea Milner

reviews.text: For the most part, it’s a quiet film touched with melancholy and calm even for its category of nostalgic reverie, a quality which makes the occasional intrusions of the present, tinged with frustration and loss, cut all the deeper.
reviews.author: Igor Fishman

reviews.text: Although quiet, the film builds to an emotionally devastating climax involving a Queen song that you’ll never hear in the same way again.
reviews.author: Glenn Sumi

reviews.text: Deftly constructed and utterly heartbreaking, Aftersun announces Charlotte Wells as an eminent storyteller of prodigious powers.
reviews.author: Pat Brown

reviews.text: A melancholy floats an inch above the surface -- the water sparkles a little too bright, that diamond sheen that's gone right before you can grab it
reviews.author: Jason Adams

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ feature debut showcases the assured hand she had already demonstrated in her short film work and enhances it further to balance tone and pace throughout a touching story of a daughter and her troubled father on holiday.
reviews.author: Jim Ross

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells uses Aftersun to show us what it’s like to unlock that box that we all keep away in a hidden dark corner of our minds. What it’s like to admit that our perfect childhood memories are just afterimages of the brightest moments.
reviews.author: Karl Delossantos

reviews.text: “Aftersun” isn’t just an honest movie about the way that we remember the people we’ve lost — fragmented, elusive, nowhere and everywhere all at once — it’s also a heart-stopping act of remembering unto itself.
reviews.author: David Ehrlich

reviews.text: Aftersun is a tender look at how we remember our loved ones.
reviews.author: Joey Magidson

reviews.text: Aftersun turns a simple and familiar story into a hypnotic and exciting audiovisual experience. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Gustavo Herrera Taboada

reviews.text: It may come on like another artfully made, ominous-seeming coming-of-age film, but it gradually deepens into remarkable exploration of memory and family and that difficult moment where parents become real people in the eyes of their children.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: Aftersun is directed with a sure hand and immense empathy.
reviews.author: Alissa Wilkinson

reviews.text: What makes Aftersun such a revelatory work is the way these inner emotions are never spelt out in dialogue, and instead are wholly expressed visually or through performance.
reviews.author: Jamie Dunn

reviews.text: An assured, aching, vibrant debut by Wells, “Aftersun” is a shattering remembrance of a father by his daughter.
reviews.author: Robert Daniels

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells has struck gold with her young discovery, Frankie Corio, who delivered one of the best and most lived-in performances in the festival’s entire lineup.
reviews.author: Kent Turner

reviews.text: A film that positively hums with atmosphere and glows with its maker’s promise.
reviews.author: Raphael Abraham

reviews.text: Thanks to Wells' wonderfully human characters, astute direction, and stellar performances, "Aftersun" truly is about the little moments that seem insignificant at the time but become the precious stuff we treasure as adults.
reviews.author: Luke Hearfield

reviews.text: Aftersun is both a rich sensory experience and unbearably sad. It’s also one of the best debuts to play at the Cannes Film Festival in years.
reviews.author: Rory O'Connor

reviews.text: Mescal's balanced portrayal of a hearty sufferer grounds the story with paradigmatic believability.
reviews.author: Savina Petkova

reviews.text: A moving, confident, striking, altogether splendid film.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: Aftersun is a flawless debut from the Scottish filmmaker. What she does next will be of great interest.
reviews.author: Andrew Murray

reviews.text: What really sets the film apart is the way it subtly communicates an enormous sadness lurking just beneath the surface.
reviews.author: Donald Clarke

reviews.text: A beautiful little anti-history. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Mariona Borrull

reviews.text: A genuine triumph of a film. With natural and nuanced performances Aftersun is a bright star in the cinematic sky, a film of real beauty.
reviews.author: Jo-Ann Titmarsh

reviews.text: The performances are extraordinary, managing to capture a naturalism which is utterly convincing. It’s difficult to think of a father/daughter relationship portrayed so touchingly and apparently allergic to cliche.
reviews.author: John Bleasdale

reviews.text: The saving grace is Corio who, in a superb and memorable debut film performance, brings some much-needed naturalism and grace to proceedings.
reviews.author: David Jenkins

reviews.text: The intention of those big, intense moments is to do justice to the magnitude of some very personal and powerful emotions. In that regard, “Aftersun” is a tonic — particularly at a festival where art films are generally cold and polite
reviews.author: Elena Lazic

reviews.text: An exquisite revelation, Aftersun, produced by Barry Jenkins, is the type of movie from which you don’t walk away the same person.
reviews.author: Carlos Aguilar

reviews.text: It’s a film of such restraint, oblique observation, and poised naturalism that the wallop of this feeling is quite unexpected. It heralds Wells as someone with a Joanna-Hogg-like career path beckoning right ahead, paved by a sensibility all her own.
reviews.author: Tim Robey

reviews.text: Wells’ measured but relentless probing, her careful peeling away of the layers of this intimate piece, mark her out as one of the most promising new voices in British cinema in recent years.
reviews.author: Fionnuala Halligan

reviews.text: Wells’s movie ripples and shimmers like a swimming pool of mystery; the way Wells captures mood and moment, never labouring the point or forcing the pace, reminded me of the young Lucrecia Martel.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: The very subject of Wells’ feature is the gap between the sensory detail of a sun-drenched vacation and the unknowable interior lives of the characters. The result is a spellbinding duet by Mescal and Frankie Corio.
reviews.author: Sheri Linden

reviews.text: Charlotte Wells’ sensuous, sharply moving debut shows that no amount of pool time and fruity drinks and Macarena dance-alongs can keep either the past or future at bay.
reviews.author: Guy Lodge

reviews.text: While this is not explicitly autobiographical, it certainly feels like a very personal piece of work, and all the better for it. Oh, and the 1990s pop soundtrack is a joy.
reviews.author: Anna Smith

synopsis: At a fading vacation resort, 11-year-old Sophie treasures rare time together with her loving and idealistic father, Calum (Paul Mescal). As a world of adolescence creeps into view, beyond her eye Calum struggles under the weight of life outside of fatherhood. Twenty years later, Sophie's tender recollections of their last holiday become a powerful and heartrending portrait of their relationship, as she tries to reconcile the father she knew with the man she didn't, in Charlotte Wells' superb and searingly emotional debut film.
